transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-11
Start time: 16:02 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (recording paused ~none)
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Daniel Kim (Triton Head of ML), Rita Alvarez (Triton CTO), Marcus Hall (Triton Infra)

Summary:
Short discovery focused on cost/unit economics across Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private options. Triton's primary concerns: per-token unit cost at scale, batching and KV/prefix caching effects on e2e latency, budget constraints for Q2, and compliance (KMS / SOC2). Discussed potential pilot and benchmarking plan.

Topics:
- Current stack and traffic
- Cost targets and budget
- Tradeoffs: latency vs cost, batching impacts
- Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private operations and security
- Next steps and pilot plan

Transcript (timestamps are approximate):
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:03] Daniel Kim: Yep good here, thanks Alex.
[00:05] Rita Alvarez: All good.
[00:07] Alex Chen: Great. Quick intros, I'll be the AE on this, Sofia our SE will cover cost/pricing and benchmark questions. Over to you Sofia.
[00:15] Sofia Martinez: Thanks Alex. Hi Triton team, thanks for the time. We want to focus on your cost constraints today and walk through how Redwood's levers — batching, prefix/KV cache, quant profiles, and Dedicated sizing — change per-token economics. Quick question up front: what's your current RPS and typical prompt/response length?
[00:35] Marcus Hall: So right now in prod we average about 20 RPS across Europe and US, spikes to 120 during market open. Payloads are variable, prompt around 80 tokens, response ~150 tokens on average. We're being conservative with budget — target for Q2 is to keep inference costs under $0.60 per thousand completions, otherwise finance will balk.
[00:56] Daniel Kim: To add, we run an in-house cache layer but it's mostly for embeddings; not much prefix caching for seq models yet.
[01:07] Sofia Martinez: Okay helpful. So two immediate levers: batching (improves throughput) and prefix/KV caching (reduces repeated token decoding). On Hosted Redwood, our per-token pricing tiers are published but effective cost depends on how much batching you can safely do given latency SLOs and on cache hit rates.
[01:27] Rita Alvarez: Can you speak to the numbers? Like published per-token vs what we might see?
[01:31] Sofia Martinez: Published hosted list price for our 70B-ish model is $0.0032 per 1k input tokens and $0.0066 per 1k output tokens — those are ballpark; actual discounts and committed throughput change that. For Dedicated, unit cost can drop significantly because of reserved capacity and being able to run larger batch sizes and model variants (quantized). We've seen customers cut per-token spend by 35-60% moving to Dedicated depending on utilization and batchability.
[02:01] Daniel Kim: 35-60% is a big range. Our constraint is 99th percentile tail latency under 350ms for interactive flows. How does batching affect that?
[02:11] Sofia Martinez: Right, that's the tradeoff. Continuous batching increases throughput per GPU but can add a batching window. With our runtime you can configure max batch latency to 20-40ms for interactive — that typically keeps p99 within your 350ms budget. If you need stricter tail latency, you can route a percentage of traffic to lower-latency nodes or use a smaller model variant.
[02:34] Marcus Hall: How about prefix caching? If we re-use a lot of context, what's the savings?
[02:38] Sofia Martinez: If you have high prefix reuse, KV cache can avoid re-decoding the prefix entirely. In practice the delta depends on how much of the token stream is repeated. For example, in customer benchmarks where 40% of tokens were repeated across requests, overall token compute dropped ~30%, which maps roughly to a 30% drop in token billing for compute component — hosted billing still charges per-token but effective tokens served decrease because we do less compute.
[03:02] Rita Alvarez: Wait you said hosted billing charges per-token; how does cache change billed tokens?
[03:07] Sofia Martinez: Good point. On Hosted we meter tokens as seen by the endpoint. If the cache eliminates generation of repeated tokens at the runtime level, the endpoint still reports consumed tokens differently depending on configuration; we have a mechanism to credit customers for cached prefixes on Dedicated and Private deployments. On Hosted we can apply usage adjustments for predictable caching patterns under contract. We'll flag that as something to include in contract work.
[03:33] Daniel Kim: So for our planning, we need to understand two scenarios: Hosted with committed discounts and Dedicated with reserved nodes. Also private on our VPC might be required for compliance. Do you have a sample ROI calc?
[03:47] Sofia Martinez: Yes — I'll send a cost model spreadsheet, but rough numbers: with your profile (avg 20 RPS, spike 120), if you stay on Hosted with a 30% cache hit and moderate batching you might land at ~$0.45 per 1k completions effective. With Dedicated and 70% utilization plus quantization (INT8/4) you could be at ~$0.18-0.30 per 1k. Private will look similar to Dedicated for pure compute but has added ops/infra and license costs.
[04:18] Marcus Hall: Those Dedicated numbers assume we can hit 70% utilization. Our pattern is spiky — will autoscaling handle bursts and maintain SLAs?
[04:26] Sofia Martinez: Yes, Dedicated supports reserved pools plus burst capacity. With autoscaling policies you can maintain baseline throughput and scale for spikes. There's also smart routing so lower-cost nodes can be used during non-critical times. For very spiky workloads we recommend a hybrid: host a baseline on Dedicated and overflow to Hosted during extreme peaks.
[04:45] Rita Alvarez: Security questions — we need SOC2, KMS integration, and audit logs for compliance. Also interested in private deployment options.
[04:53] Alex Chen: On security, we have SOC2 Type II and ISO docs. For Private we offer VPC-hosted control plane or on-prem package, and we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management. We'll share the security pack after this call.
[05:10] Daniel Kim: Great. On performance, can we run a small benchmark? 1k requests with our typical prompt/response distribution and measure p50/p95/p99 and effective spend?
[05:19] Sofia Martinez: Absolutely. We can provision a Dedicated test cluster or run on Hosted with a test project. For the tightest numbers and caching behavior we'd prefer Dedicated test cluster so we can measure cache hit impacts. We typically cap such pilots to 1 week and scale config as needed.
[05:33] Marcus Hall: For the pilot what do you need from us?
[05:36] Sofia Martinez: Sample traffic trace, a couple representative prompts, target latency SLOs, and whether you want to enable KV/prefix caching for the test. Also let us know committed throughput or budget cap.
[05:47] Marcus Hall: We can share a day's trace and agree a budget cap. Finance wants a cap of $6k for the pilot.
[05:54] Alex Chen: That should be fine, we can design the pilot to stay within that. We'll propose a config that emphasizes caching and batching to show cost delta.
[06:03] Daniel Kim: One more — how do you price model variants and quantized models? If we use an INT8 quant model, is it cheaper on Hosted too?
[06:12] Sofia Martinez: On Hosted we expose multiple model variants; the price per-token can vary by model. Lower-precision or distilled variants are priced lower. On Dedicated you have more control and can run quantized versions with lower GPU memory and higher throughput, which reduces effective cost. Exact pricing for each variant is negotiable and often tied to commit level.
[06:31] Rita Alvarez: Any hidden fees — network egress, storage, etc?
[06:34] Alex Chen: For Hosted, network egress follows cloud provider rules; we surface those. There are optional add-ons like extended logs retention, advanced observability, or premium SLA which are extra. Dedicated and Private have clear licensing and infra costs included in the quote. We'll call those out in the spreadsheet.
[06:51] Daniel Kim: Competitors question — we evaluated OpenAI and Anthropic. Anthropic looked cheaper for pure API but we worried about vendor lock-in and lack of on-prem option. Thoughts?
[07:02] Sofia Martinez: We're seeing similar — Anthropic/OpenAI are strong for simple API consumption, but teams needing private deployment, advanced caching, and predictable economics often choose Dedicated/private solutions. We also help with migration patterns so you can fallback to compatible model variants.
[07:15] [crosstalk] Marcus Hall: Sorry, one workflow question — if we enable prefix caching how does that integrate with our existing redis layer?
[07:19] Sofia Martinez: Good Q. We have two patterns: edge caching (your Redis) that dedups requests before hitting the model, and runtime KV cache that stores model KV states. They can coexist; in pilot we'll instrument both to show combined effect. We'll also provide guidance on eviction policies.
[07:36] Rita Alvarez: Ok this is useful. Can you quantify end-to-end latency when cache hits versus misses?
[07:40] Sofia Martinez: Cache hits typically shave off 25-60% of total CPU/GPU work depending on how much prefix is saved. In practice, for your prompt sizes, a cache hit could drop p50 from ~260ms to ~140ms and p99 from 540ms to 260ms in our internal tests (these numbers depend on infra and network).
[07:59] Daniel Kim: That's promising. For the ROI calc please show: Hosted base vs Hosted with committed discount vs Dedicated (reserved) vs Private (VPC with patch ops cost).
[08:10] Sofia Martinez: Will do. We'll add separate lines for quantization and caching assumptions.
[08:14] Marcus Hall: On SLAs — what's the typical uptime and support level for Dedicated?
[08:18] Alex Chen: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime, usually 99.9% for reserved clusters, with a named CSM and priority support tiers. We'll attach the SLA doc.
[08:27] Rita Alvarez: Anything else on billing granularity? We want per-route breakdown because some routes are low-value and should be routed to cheaper model variants.
[08:35] Sofia Martinez: Console provides per-route/model dashboards and token-level cost breakdown. You can set routing policies to send low-priority traffic to cheaper models or to batch them differently.
[08:44] Daniel Kim: Ok good. Can you sketch a recommended path for us?
[08:47] Alex Chen: Recommended: 1) Pilot on Dedicated test cluster with your trace (stay within $6k) to measure caching/batching gains and tail latency. 2) Use pilot results to compute economics; if Dedicated ROI > 35% savings and meets SLOs, move to reserved capacity with burst to Hosted. 3) If compliance requires, evaluate Private VPC after pilot.
[09:07] Rita Alvarez: Sounds reasonable. Timeline? We want a decision by end of March.
[09:11] Alex Chen: We'll try to get the pilot plan and cost spreadsheet to you within 48 hours; pilot could start as early as next week depending on your readiness.
[09:19] Daniel Kim: Ok we'll gather traces and confirm pilot budget.
[09:22] [silence 10s]
[09:32] Alex Chen: Any final Qs?
[09:34] Marcus Hall: None from me.
[09:35] Rita Alvarez: No.
[09:36] Daniel Kim: All good. Thanks.
[09:37] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up.
